evidence.field: file description, source, reuse terms, and version history
evidence.text: Commons identifies 工-seal.svg as a Shuowen seal-script rendering of 工, links it to the 27.5DE5 image on Academia Sinica’s 工 page, and says the underlying Sinica image is CC0; Commons also labels the SVG public domain and says attribution is appreciated but not required. The file history shows uploads in 2010 and an update in 2017. The page verifies the drawing’s identity and claimed script style, but it is a modern digital rendering rather than an artifact image.
evidence.title: File:工-seal.svg - Wikimedia Commons

evidence.text: The character-specific page labels the displayed form 小篆 and 說文‧工部, and identifies the regular-script form as 工. This supports using a seal-script glyph as a labeled historical form; it does not establish the early graph’s referent.
evidence.title: 小學堂字形

evidence.field: file description, linked source record, artifact citation, and reuse terms
evidence.text: Commons identifies 工-oracle.svg as 工 in Shang oracle-script style, links the drawing to Academia Sinica’s 42.E325 image record, and marks it CC0/public domain. This is a modern vector illustration, not a photograph of an oracle-bone inscription; Commons’ character label and source link establish its intended identity and provenance lead, but do not independently verify the specific artifact reading or the graph’s pictured object.
evidence.title: File:工-oracle.svg - Wikimedia Commons

evidence.field: file description, source, inscription citation, and reuse terms
evidence.text: Commons identifies 工-bronze.svg as 工 in Western Zhou bronze-script style and cites the 伊簋 inscription, 集成04287, as the source for the selected image. It credits the underlying source to Richard Sears’s site and points to a permission agreement; the SVG representation is labeled public domain with attribution appreciated. This is a rendered graph associated with a named inscription, not a photograph of the artifact.
evidence.title: File:工-bronze.svg - Wikimedia Commons

evidence.source: 漢語多功能字庫, Chinese University of Hong Kong
evidence.field: character graph analysis and cited examples
evidence.text: The entry presents competing interpretations: an early graph for a bladed tool, whose upper part may have had a carpenter’s-square function; a square; or a building tool. It reports oracle-bone uses as a state or place name, status or occupation, craft worker, and a whole-graph loan for 貢. It cites 多工 (合集 19433), 百工 (屯南 2525), 工(貢)冊 (合集 38310), and 工(貢)父甲三牛 (合集 27462), without displaying artifact dates. These reports do not date the first appearance of each sense or establish a single semantic chain.
evidence.title: 漢字甲骨部件分析

evidence.text: The transmitted entry explains 工 as 巧飾, describes the form as a person having 規榘, and compares it with 巫. It records 𢒄 as 古文工从彡. This historical account differs from the modern tool interpretations; it is not independent confirmation of an early pictured object. The entry does not say that 𢒄 is an ancestor of the regular graph, so the direction and type of graphic relationship should remain unresolved.
evidence.title: 說文解字「工」

evidence.source: Wiktionary, Baxter–Sagart Old Chinese reconstruction appendix
evidence.field: Old Chinese, Middle Chinese, and modern Mandarin table rows
evidence.text: The table lists 工 with modern Mandarin gōng, Middle Chinese kuwng, and Baxter–Sagart Old Chinese *kˤoŋ, for glosses ‘officer’ and ‘work’; 功 and 攻 are also listed with *kˤoŋ in this table. These are reconstructions, not direct recordings. They support close reconstructed sound correspondence in this system, but do not by themselves prove shared word origin or a semantic progression. The dossier’s local Baxter–Sagart rows for 工 independently give MC kuwng and OC *kˤoŋ for both ‘officer’ and ‘work’; the provided local row is not an external citation.
evidence.title: Appendix:Baxter-Sagart Old Chinese reconstruction

evidence.field: lookup interface and kMandarin property documentation
evidence.text: The official Unihan lookup page is available, and UAX #38 describes kMandarin as the most customary pinyin reading, intended for collation and transliteration. The character-specific lookup did not expose an inspectable row in this research. The provided local Unihan row gives 工 kMandarin gōng, but the unavailable row page means that value is not asserted here as externally verified; it is current metadata, not historical phonological evidence.
evidence.title: Unihan Database Lookup

evidence.text: The specification identifies kMandarin as an informative reading property containing the most customary pinyin reading; when only one value is present it applies to both simplified and traditional Chinese contexts. This describes the dataset’s scope, not the ancient pronunciation of 工.
evidence.title: UAX #38: Unicode Han Database (Unihan)

search_audit.outcome: Search returned the Baxter–Sagart table and project materials. Opened the appendix and inspected the 工, 功, 攻, and 貢 rows; the dedicated module and PDF did not open in this browser session.

The direct character-specific Unihan URL failed. Opened Unicode’s general Unihan lookup and UAX #38 property documentation, but did not retrieve an inspectable 工 kMandarin row. Local row supplied as gōng is therefore not presented as an externally verified row.

gaps: The Commons page for the supplied candidate Shuowen Seal Radical 147.svg did not load, and the exact Commons imageinfo API URL was inaccessible. Unlike 工-seal.svg, no external character identity, original URL, or reuse terms could be verified for that candidate; do not select it from the local file alone.

Browser attempts to fetch original SVGs and thumbnails failed or returned no inspectable image block. File-page metadata and source links support the labeled vector illustrations, but direct pixel inspection was not completed in this interface.

The precise ancient object represented by 工 remains disputed. The inspected paleographic source reports blade/tool, square, and building-tool interpretations; no inspected primary artifact photograph or independently published specialist analysis resolved the disagreement.

The proposed tool’s original spoken name and pronunciation are not independently recoverable from the inspected evidence. 工’s reconstructed pronunciation cannot be used to infer the name of the depicted object.

The CUHK entry supplies inscription identifiers but no dates for those individual examples. Earliest dated attestation of the graph and of place-name, status/title, craft-worker, work, achievement, and 貢-loan uses remains undetermined here.

The path from a possible tool depiction to craft, occupation, work, skill, and achievement is not securely established. The Shuowen semantic explanation differs from the modern paleographic interpretations, and gloss lists alone cannot supply chronology.

工(貢) is reported as a whole-graph loan, not an internal sound-component analysis. The sound relation at the time of borrowing and the independent historical reading of 貢 were not verified in this pass.
The relationship between Shuowen’s 𢒄 and 工 is not classified by direction in the inspected source; do not assert an ancestor-to-descendant relation merely because the entry calls 𢒄 an ancient form.
The required official Unihan character-specific page did not expose an inspectable kMandarin row; current reading is available only from the supplied local row and other inspected secondary material.
